posts.quote: GRANDPA DREW AN OUTLINE AROUND EVERY TOOL ON THE PEGBOARD, SO YOU ALWAYS KNEW WHAT WAS MISSING.
posts.caption: Grandpa's workshop was the one room in the house with a rule posted on the wall, and the rule was drawn in black marker. Every hammer, saw, and pair of pliers hung inside its own outline, like a chalk figure at the scene of a very organized crime. If you borrowed something, you could see the empty shape sitting there, patiently waiting. Nobody ever had to be told who had the level. By supper he would stand in the doorway, look at the board, and say the name of the culprit without turning around.
posts.first: I borrowed his tape measure once and kept it three days, and that empty outline did more to teach me about returning things than any lecture could have. I still hang my own tools that way. The outlines are a little crooked, but every one of them gets used.

posts.quote: A SICK DAY MEANT GINGER ALE, SALTINES, AND A LITTLE BELL BY THE BED THAT YOU WERE NOT SUPPOSED TO ABUSE.
posts.caption: The thermometer came out of the drawer, and a verdict was reached before you had even opened your eyes. If it said what Mom hoped it wouldn't, you were staying home, and the rest of the day moved at a different speed. The ginger ale sat until it went flat, because flat was the only way it was allowed. The saltines were laid out on a plate like medicine, and the bell was for emergencies only. By noon you had rung it four times, and the emergencies were getting a little thin.
posts.first: My mother wrapped a cold washcloth around my forehead and told me to lie still, which was harder than being sick. I could hear her moving around the kitchen all day, and every time I rang that bell she showed up anyway. I never once heard her sigh.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the fuel oil man)
posts.quote: THE FUEL OIL MAN / A LONG HOSE, A HEAVY BOOT, AND A TANK THAT GURGLED FOR HALF AN HOUR
posts.caption: You could hear him before you saw him, a heavy truck idling at the curb and a hose dragging across the frozen lawn. He walked it to the pipe on the side of the house, pushed the nozzle in, and then stood there stamping his boots while the tank filled. From the basement came a long, slow gurgle, like the house was drinking. He wrote the gallons on a ticket, tore it off, and tucked it in the storm door. For the rest of the winter that tank was the only thing anyone in the family worried about.
posts.first: Our tank sat in the corner of the basement beside the washer, with a little glass gauge that Dad checked every morning on his way to the furnace. He tapped it with his fingernail like he was testing a melon. If the needle sat low he got quiet at supper, and we all understood why.

posts.quote: The good tablecloth came out for Sunday and holidays, and it was ironed the night before.
posts.first: It was white, with a lace edge, and it had one faint stain in the corner that my mother had been working on since before I was born. Nobody ever spilled on it, because everybody could feel it was watching. After supper it went right back in the drawer, folded in thirds, and the table went back to being a table.

posts.quote: AFTER LUNCH THE TEACHER READ US ONE CHAPTER, AND THE WHOLE ROOM WENT QUIETER THAN CHURCH.
posts.caption: It was the best twenty minutes of the day, and nobody had to say so. Lunch was over, the playground dust was still on your shoes, and the teacher pulled a heavy book out of her desk drawer. She never used a special voice. She just read, and the story got into the room the way warm air does. When she closed the cover on a cliffhanger and said that was all for today, the whole class groaned in perfect unison. Then we went right back to arithmetic, still half inside that book.
posts.first: My fourth-grade teacher read us the same story every fall, and by the second year I could tell when she was about to skip a page. I never said so, because it would have ended the whole arrangement. I still remember where I was sitting for every chapter.

posts.quote: THE BOWL OF WALNUTS CAME OUT IN NOVEMBER WITH A CRACKER AND A PICK, AND THE SHELLS COVERED THE NEWSPAPER BY BEDTIME.
posts.caption: The bowl showed up on the coffee table the first week of November, and it stayed until somebody bought a Christmas tree. The newspaper under it was there to catch the shells, but it never caught all of them. Dad cracked the hard ones with the steel cracker, and the rest of us dug through the pieces with the little pick. A whole walnut half, unbroken, was treated like a minor miracle. By bedtime the newspaper looked like a battlefield, and someone always had a sliver stuck in their sock.
posts.first: My grandfather had a pair of walnut trees behind the barn, and he would fill a pillowcase every fall and leave it on our porch without a word. We never found out when he did it. The pillowcase just appeared.

posts.character: Work and family (the lunch pail note)
posts.quote: DAD'S LUNCH PAIL HAD A NOTE FROM MOM UNDER THE SANDWICH, AND HE KEPT EVERY ONE OF THEM.
posts.caption: He worked the line at the plant for thirty-one years, and the lunch pail went with him every one of them. Mom packed it the night before, a sandwich wrapped in wax paper, an apple, a slice of cake when there was cake. Under the sandwich she tucked a note, usually a few words about the grocery list or the weather. He read it at the break table by himself, with the same small smile, and then he folded it into his shirt pocket. When he retired, my sister found them in a cigar box in the closet, thousands of little pieces of paper held together with rubber bands.
posts.first: The notes were almost never anything serious. One said the dog had thrown up on the porch and she'd handled it. Another said only, see you at six. I read through that box on a rainy afternoon, and I understood what a marriage looked like.

posts.quote: The grocer added up your groceries on a paper bag with a stubby pencil, and he was never off by a penny.
posts.first: He kept the pencil tucked behind his ear and wrote the numbers in a quick column down the side of the bag. Nobody ever checked his math, because there was no reason to. If the total came to a few cents over, he rounded down and handed you the bag without saying a word.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the chimney sweep)
posts.quote: THE CHIMNEY SWEEP / A TALL BRUSH, A DROP CLOTH, AND A HOUSE THAT SMELLED LIKE SOOT FOR A DAY
posts.caption: Every fall a man in a black cap rang the bell and asked where the fireplace was. He spread a canvas cloth across the rug as if he were setting up a stage, then fed a long brush up the flue joint by joint. From somewhere far above came a scratching, and a little soot drifted down into the hearth like black snow. When he finished he rolled up the cloth, shook out his hands, and wrote the date on a card. The house smelled like a burnt match for a day, and Dad said that was how you knew it was safe.
posts.first: Ours used to sing a little in the flue when the wind came from the north, and Mom said that was the house clearing its throat. The sweep was a quiet fellow with a gray mustache, and he drank his coffee standing up. I never saw him sit down in our house, not once.

posts.quote: THE STRING OF CHRISTMAS LIGHTS CAME OUT OF THE BOX IN ONE KNOT, AND DAD SPENT HALF AN HOUR PRETENDING HE WASN'T FRUSTRATED.
posts.caption: The box came down from the closet shelf the first weekend of December, and inside it was the same knot as last year. Dad lowered himself onto the carpet with a sigh he insisted wasn't a sigh. He found one end and followed it, found the other end and lost it, and told us everything was fine in the voice that meant otherwise. Mom stood in the doorway with a dish towel, wise enough to say nothing. After thirty minutes the cord finally lay straight, and the one bulb that didn't work turned out to be the one in the middle.
posts.first: We tested every bulb on that string one at a time, and I held the spare. Dad never once raised his voice, but he did say a word I had never heard before. I've since had my own knot, and I think I finally understand.
